newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine Yankee bond delay right choice-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Philippine Yankee bond delay right choice-analysts.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank was probably wise to delay its planned Yankee bond issue given the state of the U.S. market and a less voracious appetite recently for Philippine paper, analysts said on Wednesday.
Earlier the Central Bank said it had postponed the launch, originally set for Tuesday, of $1.0 billion in 30- and 100-year bonds, citing poor market conditions.

"It takes quite a bit of guts to reschedule. You open yourself to all sorts of criticism. That tells me it is in fact an exercise in prudence," chief economist of the Bankers Association of the Philippines, Johnny Ravalo, said.
His group has been a strong defender of the bond which has come under some local criticism for what Ravalo called unfounded fears that the issue would simply add to the country's debt burden.
The Philippine government said it could quickly come back to the market.

"It was clear from our roadshow that investors found the Philippine credit quality highly acceptable and that this was not the cause of pricing difficulties," Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said in a letter to President Fidel Ramos.

"With the completion of U.S. SEC registration requirements and the investor roadshow, we can therefore quickly come back to the market to launch the...bond at a price much more favourable and appropriate to us than what can be obtained under present difficult overall market conditions," Singson wrote.
"I think it's a wise decision on the governor's part," Citibank Manila head of capital markets, Andrew Alcid said.

"If all they wanted to do was to raise money they probably could have shortened the tenor and got a deal done but that's not what they really wanted to do," he added, noting the government was trying to establish a benchmark for Philippine borrowers.
He was confident the bond would eventually be issued.
Some analysts estimate that Philippine companies and state agencies could tap international markets for up to $1.5 billion this year.
But they noted apprehension among some investors.
"There is an impression that Philippine assets have been kind of pricey," one analyst said.
"The appetite for the Philippines has cooled recently. There is a little bit of concern -- not well-founded -- that the Philippines is going the same way as Thailand," he added.
"We're still positive generally on the fundamentals and even the politics,' he said.
Campaigning is already underway for the Philippine presidential election in a year's time with no clear picture on who will replace Ramos.
